en: The Contemplation Gate of the Perfect Interfusion of the Three Sages, composed by the Śramaṇa Chengguan.
Now, when the supreme sages observe humanity and establish their teachings, their words are not spoken in vain; they manifest through the pointing of a finger, touching upon every matter.
All these are interconnected.

Because there was the profound virtue of the "Cause," he was prompted to reveal the two meanings by which the Two Sages symbolize the Dharma, and thus composed the *Three Sages' Perfectly Interfused Contemplation*.
The contemplative wisdom of a single hair is difficult to fully comprehend; therefore, [he wrote this].
Relying briefly upon the scriptural teachings and principles, I have set forth these essential outlines; I hope only that those of far-reaching insight will empty their minds and seek them therein.
As for the "Three Sages," they are the Original Teacher, Vairocana Tathāgata, and the two Great Bodhisattvas, Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī.

When the Great Awakened One appeared in the world, he was assisted by beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; yet, within the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the two sages alone are singled out as the foremost leaders. This was done to entrust them with the manifestation of the Dharma, and it was not for nothing.
Now, two gates will be briefly elucidated:
first, manifesting through mutual contrast;
second, revealing perfection through mutual integration.
Furthermore, within the first section:
among the three sages, two sages constitute the cause and the Tathāgata constitutes the fruit.
Since the fruit gives rise to speech and thought, we shall here speak of the two causes.
If one awakens to the profound subtlety of these two causes, then one will know the deep mystery of the ocean of fruition.
Now, the Dharma-gates of these two sages can be briefly categorized into three pairs:
first, the pair of that which is able to believe and that which is believed.

This means that Samantabhadra represents the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) which is the object of faith—the tathāgatagarbha while still enmeshed in defilements. Thus, the *Prajñāpāramitā-naya-sūtra* states:
"All sentient beings are the tathāgatagarbha."
Because the essential body of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva is all-pervasive, the reason he enters the Tathāgatagarbha-kāya-samādhi at the very first assembly is intended to convey this meaning.

Mañjuśrī represents the mind capable of faith; as the *Buddhanāma Sūtra* states, "All Buddhas give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment because of Mañjuśrī," which signifies that [enlightenment] is produced in dependence upon faith.
That Sudhana first beholds [Mañjuśrī] and gives rise to the Great Mind is because he is at the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*).
As the *Sūtra* says:
"The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī gives birth to all bodhisattvas without ceasing."
However, regarding faith, there is merely faith without yet having seen the non-dual principle between that which is believed and that which is realized.
Therefore, how could there be an initial Samantabhadra from whom faith might first arise?
Since principle consists solely of ultimate vision, Mañjuśrī is placed at the beginning and Samantabhadra at the end.
Second, by correlating understanding (*jñāna*) with practice (*caryā*):
Samantabhadra represents the myriad practices that arise; as all the various sūtras state:
This is because of the "conduct of Samantabhadra.
Mañjuśrī represents the wisdom that initiates [practice], as he thoroughly understands both phenomena and principle and exhausts all skillful means.
As Maitreya said:

"It is because it was through the majestic spiritual power of Mañjuśrī that you were previously able to see the various spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), hear of the bodhisattva practices, and enter the gates of liberation."
Furthermore, it says:
"Because Mañjuśrī is always the teacher of all bodhisattvas.
And it further says:
"By the power of Mañjuśrī’s mental resolve.
Third, the correspondence between principle and wisdom:
Samantabhadra represents the realized Dharma-realm, which is the Tathāgatagarbha free from entanglements; this is because "Sudhana enters his body."
It is further stated:
"Because one attains the body that is ultimately equal throughout the three periods of time.
That a single hair is vast and boundless is because it accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
The physical form of Samantabhadra is like empty space.
Furthermore, the statement that one attains the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-pāramitā*) upon seeing Samantabhadra clarifies that wisdom is generated by relying upon the principle (*tattva*).
Mañjuśrī represents the great wisdom that realizes [the truth], for the name of the Buddha whom he originally served is Akṣobhyajñāna (Immovable Wisdom).
As Maitreya said:
"Mañjuśrī has always been the mother of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas."
This is because among all the sūtras, the dharma-gates taught by Mañjuśrī predominantly reveal the purport of Prajñāpāramitā;
furthermore, it is said:
"Born from the great ocean of Mañjuśrī’s wisdom."
One sees Mañjuśrī first and only then sees Samantabhadra; this manifests that one possesses wisdom, for it is through wisdom that one realizes the principle.
Therefore, the ancient masters inscribed Mañjuśrī as "wisdom illuminating the non-dual aspect."
The phrase "not viewing bodily marks" signifies that ultimate wisdom is profoundly deep; for both mind and object have already ceased, and both faith and understanding are simultaneously transcended.

Furthermore, because principle reveals essence and function, and wisdom distinguishes the provisional and the real, Mañjuśrī’s two types of wisdom serve as the realization of Samantabhadra’s essence and function.
Regarding this single gate, when the ancient masters personally inquired about it, the Tripiṭaka Master said:
"There is a sūtra that speaks of it, but it has not yet been transmitted to this region.
Furthermore, this gate also represents both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*); for the principle is fundamentally quiescent, and wisdom is itself insight (*prajñā*).
This also expresses the essence and its function: Samantabhadra’s principle is quiescent and serves as the essence of the mind, while Mañjuśrī’s wisdom-illumination constitutes the great function.
Second, regarding the manifestation of perfection through mutual integration, there are two parts:
first, clarifying that the dharma-gates of the two sages are each individually perfect and integrated.
This means that Mañjuśrī, one must rely on faith in order to be able to achieve understanding.
For if there is understanding without faith, it increases false views;
if there is faith without understanding, it prolongs ignorance.
When faith and understanding are authentic and true, one then realizes the fundamental source;
when ultimate wisdom is perfected, that ultimate wisdom reflects back upon itself and is no different from the original mind.
Therefore, at the very moment the initial aspiration for enlightenment is first conceived, one attains perfect awakening.

Furthermore, because the wisdom of the preliminary expedient means does not depart from the essence of wisdom, the name "Mañjuśrī" in the subsequent section signifies wisdom that illuminates the non-dual aspect.

Since the illumination of faith is no different from wisdom, he extends his right hand from his formless body; thus, through these three matters, Mañjuśrī’s manifestations are harmoniously integrated and subtly interpenetrating.
Next, regarding the mutual fusion of the three aspects of Samantabhadra:
if there were no practice within principle, the principle would ultimately never be manifested;
by giving rise to practice based upon the essence, the practice necessarily accords with that essence.
Because one realizes the principle through practice, there is no principle outside of practice;
because one manifests practice through the principle, there is no practice outside of the principle.

Accordingly, whatever principle is realized is necessarily such that realizing one is to realize all. Therefore, seeing the Dharma-gate attained within a single hair-pore of Samantabhadra exceeds the previous [attainment] by an unspeakable multiple, for this is the function that is identical to the essence itself.
The "Hairs" and "Pores" Dharma-gates give rise to an inexhaustible dependent origination; through these, the three matters of Samantabhadra interpenetrate in layers upon layers.
Second, regarding the mutual fusion of the two sages' Dharma-gates:
this means that one must rely on faith before one can know the faith of the Dharma-realm.
Because believing while not trusting in principle is itself heterodox;
for subject and object are non-dual.
It is not the state of a bodhisattva to lack faith that one’s own mind possesses the Tathāgatagarbha.

Next, one must rely upon understanding (*jñāna*) before being able to initiate practice; when practice arises in accordance with understanding, such that practice does not differ from understanding, then understanding and practice are non-dual.

Furthermore, since wisdom (*prajñā*) is the function of principle (*tattva*), one realizes principle to constitute wisdom, which in turn illuminates that principle; when wisdom and principle are in profound union, it is called true wisdom, and thus principle and wisdom are non-dual.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"There is no suchness outside of wisdom that can be realized by wisdom, nor is there a suchness outside of wisdom that is entered by wisdom.
Furthermore, the quiescent illumination of the dharma-realm is called *śamatha* (calm abiding); its constant illumination within quiescence is called *vipaśyanā* (insight).
When one contemplates the ultimate limit of numerical calculation, it wondrously accords with quiescence; this is the non-duality of meditative concentration and wisdom (*samādhi-prajñā*).
Furthermore, the function of the essence is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*), and the essence of the function is called "principle" (*li*); thus, essence and function are non-dual.

Therefore, the three matters of Mañjuśrī’s interpenetration are profound and subtle; these are precisely the three matters of Samantabhadra’s layered entry. These two are not different, and this is called the practice of Samantabhadra’s Indra’s Net.

Therefore, the "Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra" reverses the approach of various other scriptures by extensively revealing the perfect fusion of principle and phenomena as the practice of Samantabhadra;
it is not merely a matter of phenomenal practice that is called the practice of Samantabhadra.

Since the two sages are mutually fused yet not designated as "Mañjuśrī-practitioner," this is because wisdom is subsumed within principle; as they constitute the single dharma-realm of the one mind, taking up one part fully encompasses the whole.

When these two noble Dharma-gates are thus mutually integrated, then Samantabhadra’s causes are fulfilled; transcending all marks and severing all words, one sinks into the ocean of cause and effect. This is named Vairocana, whose light shines everywhere, for it is realized only through correspondence with the realization itself.
In the "Dharmadhātu Chapter," the verses praising the Buddha’s virtues following Samantabhadra manifest the characteristics of the fruition (*phala-lakṣaṇa*).
At the beginning of the chapter, the Tathāgata enters samādhi and manifests signs without speaking, signifying that the realized truth is beyond words;
whereas Samantabhadra elucidates it and emits light to induce awakening, signifying that the realizing wisdom is beyond words.
That Mañjuśrī reveals and elucidates this is precisely the intended meaning.
If one were to combine the dharma-gates of these three sages to form the title of the scripture:
Samantabhadra represents "Great," for the essence of the principle he realizes encompasses all things without exception.
Mañjuśrī represents the *vaipulya* (extensive teachings), which is the wisdom of ultimate principle (*li*), functioning as its activity.

Furthermore, Samantabhadra represents the "pervasive" (*tong*), wherein principle encompasses both essence and function; he is pervasive because he is the object of realization. Thus, both Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra constitute the ten thousand practices of the *Avataṃsaka*: peeling, spreading, faith, wisdom, understanding, and practice are all the causal "flowers" used for "adornment."
Because its essence is fundamentally quiescent, Śānta is "Buddha.
Because it universally perfects all causes and realizes the supreme essence and function, it is said to be "Sūtra."

Because these terms reveal the underlying principle, they encompass the title of the work without omission and exhaustively subsume the meaning of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*; furthermore, throughout the various teachings of a single lifetime, nothing exists apart from this identity of principle and wisdom.
However, the aforementioned principle-wisdom and so forth are all inseparable from the mind;
for there is no distinction between the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings.
If one can realize this within the mind, then in every thought-moment the cause will be perfected, and in every thought-moment the fruit will be fulfilled.
The "Chapter on Manifestation" states:
"A bodhisattva should know that within their own mind, in every thought-moment, there is always a Buddha attaining perfect enlightenment.
Thus, while the identity [of the internal] and difference [of the external] are one, this does not obstruct external observation; do not become mired in mere words.

If one is in accord with this contemplation, then whenever the eyes encounter objects, one will constantly see the Three Sages and the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions; for one is all, and mind and object are non-dual.
If one practices according to this, though success may not be achieved in a single lifetime, the three sages will surely be perfected.

This concludes the Contemplation Gate of the Perfect Interfusion of the Three Sages. On the twenty-first day of the eighth month of the year of the Ox (Bichū), in the second year of the Jōkyō era, it was transcribed at my lodgings in the Southern Capital.
